Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verses 1–4:

Naming of the surah

• It is called Al-Qalam (The Pen), because it opens with God's oath by the pen, which signifies the high status of the pen and what follows from the science of writing and penmanship, namely the advancement of nations and their civilizations.

From the aims of the surah

• Consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) for the harm he suffered from the polytheists, commanding him to be patient with them, showing the elevation of his rank, his nobility and the perfection of his guidance, showing the misguidance of his opponents, pointing to their stance towards his call (ﷺ), and mentioning some of their ugly qualities, as a warning against obeying them.

• Warning the polytheists of the punishment of the Hereafter and the afflictions of this world, by setting forth a parable of their ingratitude for God's blessing upon them through the story of the people of the garden, whom their might and wealth deceived, so they denied God's blessings and withheld the rights of the needy; so God removed their blessing. This is contrasted with the state of the believers who follow and fear God, combining encouragement and warning.

• Discussion of the Resurrection and its terrors, showing the powerlessness of the polytheists' gods, that they will avail them nothing in this world or the Hereafter, mentioning the state of the criminals on that grievous day, and admonishing them that what they are in of blessing is only a gradual lead-up to punishment (istidraj), and that they have no excuse for how they met the call of the Prophet (ﷺ).

[The Tafsir]

﴿Nūn﴾. The discussion of the disjointed letters has already been given at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. God swears by the pen with which the angels and people write, and by what they write of good, benefit and knowledge. You, O Messenger, are not, by the grace of God upon you through prophethood and messengership, weak of mind or foolish in judgment. Indeed, for what you encounter of hardships in conveying the message, you have a great reward, neither diminished nor cut off. And indeed you, O Messenger, are upon a great character, which is what the Qur'an comprises of noble morals; for adherence to the Qur'an was his disposition, he complied with its command and refrained from what it forbade.

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verse 7:

Indeed your Lord, glorified is He, is most knowing of the wretched one who has deviated from the religion of Allah and the path of guidance, and He is most knowing of the god-fearing one who has been guided to the religion of truth.
So stand firm, O Messenger, in what you are upon, opposing those who deny, and do not obey them.
They wish that you would be lenient with them and flatter them regarding some of what they are upon, so that they would be lenient toward you.

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verses 10–15:

And do not obey, O Messenger, every man who swears too much and is contemptible, a slanderer who goes about with malicious gossip, who carries tales from one people to another to sow discord among them, who is stingy with wealth and withholds it from what is right, who is excessive in preventing good, who transgresses his limits in aggression against people and in committing what is forbidden, who is sinful in abundance, harsh in his disbelief, coarse and base, and attributed to other than his father. And because he possessed wealth and children, he became arrogant and turned away from the truth. When one of the verses of the Qur'an is recited to him, he denies them and says: "These are the fables of the ancients and their myths." Although these verses were revealed concerning some of the polytheists, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, they contain a warning to the Muslim against agreeing with anyone who has these blameworthy qualities.

We have tested the people of Makkah with hunger and famine, just as We tested the owners of the garden when they swore to one another that they would surely harvest its fruit early in the morning, so that none of the needy or others would eat from it. And they did not say, "If Allah wills."
So Allah sent down upon it a fire that burned it during the night while they were asleep, and by morning it was scorched and black, like the dark night.

They set out at the beginning of the day toward their orchard, with their evil intent of preventing the needy from its fruit, and they were fully confident of their ability to carry it out, in their own estimation.

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verse 26–33:

When they saw their garden burned, they said, "We have surely lost our way to it." But when they recognized that it was indeed their garden, they said, "Rather, we have been deprived of its produce, because of our resolve to be miserly and to withhold from the needy." The most just among them said, "Did I not tell you? Why did you not make the exception and say, 'If God wills'?" They said, after they had returned to their senses, "Glory be to our Lord, who is far removed from injustice in what has befallen us. Rather, we were wrongdoers against ourselves by abandoning the exception and by our evil intention." Then some of them turned toward others, blaming one another for abandoning the exception and for their evil intention. They said, "Woe to us! We were indeed transgressors, exceeding the limit in withholding from the poor and opposing the command of God. Perhaps our Lord will give us something better than our garden, because of our repentance and our acknowledgment of our sin. Indeed, to our Lord alone we turn with desire, hoping for pardon and seeking good." Such was the punishment with which We punished the people of the garden; so will be the punishment in this world for everyone who opposes the command of God and is miserly with the blessings God has given him, not discharging God's right in them. But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater and more severe than the punishment of this world, if only they knew. They would have restrained themselves from every cause that necessitates punishment.

**Commentary of the King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on Surah 68, verse 42:**

On the Day of Resurrection the matter will become severe and its terror intense. God, exalted is He, will come to judge between the creatures, and He will uncover His noble shin (*saq*), which nothing resembles. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord will uncover His shin, and every believing man and woman will prostrate to Him. Only those who used to prostrate in this world for show and reputation (*riya'* and *sum'ah*) will remain, and they will try to prostrate, but their backs will turn into a single plate." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Their eyes will be downcast, unable to lift them, overtaken by intense humiliation from the punishment of God. In the world they had been called to prayer to God and to worship Him, while they were healthy and able to perform it, yet they did not prostrate, out of arrogance and pride.

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verse 44–45:

"So leave Me alone with those who deny this Qur'an, O Messenger. As for them, upon Me is their recompense and retribution against them. We will provide them with wealth, children and blessings, as a gradual leading toward destruction without their realizing that it is the cause of their ruin. I will give them respite and prolong their lives, so that they may increase in sin. Indeed, My plan against the people of disbelief is strong and firm."

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verses 46–47:

Do you ask them, O Messenger, for a worldly wage for conveying the message, so that they are burdened with a heavy debt because of it? Or do they have knowledge of the unseen, so that they write down what they judge for themselves, that they are of higher standing with Allah than the believers in Him?

Be patient, O Messenger, with what your Lord has decreed and judged, including His granting them respite and delaying your victory over them. And do not be like the Companion of the Fish, who is Yunus (peace be upon him), in his anger and his lack of patience with his people, when he called out to his Lord in the darkness of the sea and the darkness of the belly of the fish, while he was filled with distress. Had it not been that a blessing from his Lord overtook him, by granting him success in repentance and accepting it, he would have been cast out from the belly of the fish onto the barren, desolate land, while he was one who deserved blame. But his Lord chose him for His message, and made him among the righteous, those whose intentions, words and deeds were sound.

Commentary of King Fahd Complex (al-Tafsir al-Muyassar) on surah 68, verse 51:

And indeed the disbelievers, when they heard the Qur'an, would almost strike you, O Messenger, with the evil eye, out of their hatred for you, were it not for Allah's protection and safeguarding of you. And they say, according to their own desires: "Indeed, he is a madman."
And the Qur'an is nothing but an admonition and a reminder for the worlds, of mankind and the jinn.
